lessons.title: Building a Cost Model: Coding the Indian Cost Stack Into a Backtest

children.text: Lessons 1 and 2 gave you every rate needed: the segment-by-segment table for STT, exchange charges, SEBI fees, and stamp duty, and the broker-dependent brokerage rule. This lesson turns that into a single Python function you can call on every simulated trade in a backtest, and validates it against the exact rupee figures worked out by hand earlier in this course.
Step 1: Encode the Rate Table as Data

The segment table from Lesson 1 becomes a plain Python dictionary. Keeping rates as data, not hardcoded inside formulas, is what makes the model easy to update when a Union Budget changes one of these numbers, exactly the risk flagged throughout this chapter.

body.caption: Segment rate table, as decimals (percent divided by 100)

children.text: Step 2: Encode Brokerage, Including the "Whichever Is Lower" Rule
Brokerage is the one piece that depends on the broker rather than the segment, so it gets its own function, matching the discount and full-service structures priced in Lesson 2.

body.caption: Broker-dependent brokerage function

children.text: One function ties the rate table and the brokerage function together, applies the buy or sell side correctly, and computes GST only on the three components it actually applies to, brokerage, exchange transaction charges, and the SEBI fee, never on STT or stamp duty, since those are themselves taxes.

body.caption: The complete per-trade cost function
body.code:
def trade_cost(trade_value, segment, side, broker="discount"):
    rates = SEGMENT_RATES[segment]
    stt = trade_value * (rates["stt_buy"] if side == "buy" else rates["stt_sell"])
    stamp_duty = trade_value * (rates["stamp_duty_buy"] if side == "buy" else rates["stamp_duty_sell"])
    exchange_txn = trade_value * rates["exchange_txn"]
    sebi_fee = trade_value * rates["sebi_fee"]
    brok = brokerage(trade_value, segment, broker)

    gst = 0.18 * (brok + exchange_txn + sebi_fee)

    total = stt + stamp_duty + exchange_txn + sebi_fee + brok + gst

    return {
        "brokerage": round(brok, 2),
        "stt": round(stt, 2),
        "exchange_txn": round(exchange_txn, 2),
        "sebi_fee": round(sebi_fee, 2),
        "stamp_duty": round(stamp_duty, 2),
        "gst": round(gst, 2),
        "total": round(total, 2),
    }

children.text: Step 4: Validate Against Numbers You Already Know

A cost function is only trustworthy once it reproduces figures you already worked out by hand. Chapter 1 priced a ₹1,00,000 delivery round trip through a discount broker at ₹118.62 on the buy side and ₹103.62 on the sell side. Running the function on the same inputs should return exactly that.

body.caption: Sanity check against the Chapter 1 worked example
body.code:
buy = trade_cost(100000, "equity_delivery", "buy", broker="discount")
sell = trade_cost(100000, "equity_delivery", "sell", broker="discount")

assert buy["total"] == 118.62, buy
assert sell["total"] == 103.62, sell

print(buy)
# {'brokerage': 0.0, 'stt': 100.0, 'exchange_txn': 2.97,
#  'sebi_fee': 0.1, 'stamp_duty': 15.0, 'gst': 0.55, 'total': 118.62}

body.text: This is the same discipline used throughout this course: build the model, then check it against a hand-worked number before trusting it inside a full backtest. A cost function with a silent unit error, rupees where the code expects percent, or premium where it expects notional, will run without crashing and quietly produce a backtest that is wrong in a new way.

children.text: Step 5: Wire It Into a Backtest Loop

body.caption: Applying the cost function to every simulated trade
body.code:
def run_backtest_with_costs(trades, broker="discount"):
    """trades: list of dicts with keys
    'value' (trade value or premium), 'segment', 'side', 'gross_pnl'
    """
    total_cost = 0.0
    net_pnl = 0.0

    for trade in trades:
        cost = trade_cost(trade["value"], trade["segment"], trade["side"], broker)
        total_cost += cost["total"]
        net_pnl += trade["gross_pnl"] - cost["total"]

    return {"total_cost": round(total_cost, 2), "net_pnl": round(net_pnl, 2)}

body.text: Three mistakes account for most broken cost models in practice: applying the cost only on entry and forgetting the exit leg, passing an option's notional exposure into a function that expects premium (Lesson 1 showed how large that error can be), and reusing one flat trade_value across every rebalance instead of recomputing it as position sizes change. Each one produces a backtest that runs cleanly and reports a plausible-looking, wrong number.

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: In the trade_cost function above, GST is computed as 0.18 * (brok + exchange_txn + sebi_fee). Why does this line leave out stt and stamp_duty?
options: GST applies to all charges without exception, this is a bug in the function
STT and stamp duty are themselves taxes, and GST is not levied on top of other taxes
STT and stamp duty are refunded at the end of the financial year, so GST would be pointless
GST only applies to intraday and F&O trades, not to STT or stamp duty on any segment
body.explanation: GST in India is charged on brokerage, exchange transaction charges, and SEBI fees, the fee-for-service components. STT and stamp duty are themselves taxes, and GST is not charged on top of other taxes, so a correct cost function must exclude both from the GST base.

body.text: A cost model is only three things: a rate table you can update without touching logic, a brokerage function that reflects your actual broker, and a formula that applies the right rate to the right side of the right segment. Validate it against numbers you have already checked by hand before trusting it inside a single backtest run.

points: Keeping rates as a data dictionary, separate from the cost formula, makes a cost model easy to update when STT, stamp duty, exchange charges, or GST rates change.
Brokerage needs its own function because it depends on the broker, not the segment, and must correctly implement flat-or-percentage, whichever-is-lower logic for discount brokers.
GST is computed only on brokerage, exchange transaction charges, and SEBI fees, never on STT or stamp duty, since those are themselves taxes.
Always validate a new cost function against a number you have already worked out by hand; a function with a silent unit error will run without crashing and still produce a wrong backtest.
